blocks.text: A hibiscus flower is bright red with a long projecting column, and bees and sunbirds visit it all morning. A maize tassel is dull green, has no scent and no nectar, and shakes clouds of pollen into the wind. Neither is decoration — each is a precisely engineered reproductive organ.

blocks.markdown:
## Parts of a flower

A flower is a shoot with four rings of modified leaves attached to a swollen base, the **receptacle**.

Working from the outside inwards: the **calyx** is the ring of green **sepals** that protected the bud. Inside it the **corolla** is the ring of **petals**, often brightly coloured and scented in insect-pollinated flowers. Then comes the **androecium**, the male part, made of **stamens**; each stamen has a stalk called a **filament** carrying an **anther** in which pollen grains are made. At the centre is the **gynoecium**, the female part, made of one or more **carpels**; each carpel has a sticky **stigma** on top, a **style** beneath it, and at the base an **ovary** containing one or more **ovules**, each with an egg cell inside.

blocks.title: Pollination
blocks.text: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. Self-pollination is transfer to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant; cross-pollination is transfer to a flower on a different plant of the same species. Pollination is not fertilisation — it only brings the gametes close enough to meet.

blocks.title: From pollination to seed
blocks.prompt: Describe what happens after a compatible pollen grain lands on the stigma of a hibiscus flower.

steps.text: The pollen grain absorbs a sugary solution from the sticky stigma and germinates, growing a pollen tube.
The pollen tube grows down through the style towards the ovary, digesting a path with enzymes and directed by chemicals released from the ovule.
The tube enters the ovule through a small opening, the micropyle, and its tip bursts, releasing two male gametes.

One male gamete fuses with the egg cell nucleus to form a diploid zygote, which will become the embryo. The other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm nucleus, which will form the food store. This is double fertilisation, and it is unique to flowering plants.
After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed, its wall hardening into the testa, and the whole ovary becomes the fruit. The petals, stamens, stigma and style wither and fall.

blocks.answer: The pollen grain germinates and its tube grows down the style to the ovule, where one male gamete fertilises the egg to give the embryo and the other forms the endosperm. The ovule then becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

blocks.markdown:
### Fruits, seeds and dispersal

Once the seed is formed it must get away from the parent, or it will germinate in the parent's shade and compete with it for light, water and mineral salts. Dispersal also lets a species colonise new ground.

- **Wind dispersal** — seeds or fruits are light, and often have wings or a parachute of hairs. Examples: *Combretum*, silk cotton, *Tridax*.
- **Animal dispersal** — either succulent, brightly coloured, edible fruits whose seeds pass out unharmed (mango, guava, pawpaw, tomato), or fruits with hooks and spines that catch on fur and clothing (*Desmodium*, burdock).
- **Water dispersal** — the fruit is buoyant, with a fibrous or air-filled layer. Example: coconut.
- **Explosive mechanism** — the dry fruit wall dries unevenly and splits violently, flinging the seeds out. Examples: *Crotalaria*, castor oil plant, okra when overripe.

blocks.title: Structural devices that promote cross-pollination
blocks.text: Cross-pollination gives more variation, so many plants avoid self-pollination structurally: unisexual flowers (pawpaw has separate male and female plants), protandry where anthers ripen before the stigma, protogyny where the stigma ripens first, self-sterility where the plant's own pollen cannot germinate on its stigma, and heterostyly where style and stamen lengths differ.

blocks.title: Ovary to fruit, ovule to seed
blocks.text: Learn these two conversions exactly. The ovary becomes the fruit; each ovule becomes a seed. It follows that a fruit with six seeds developed from an ovary that contained six ovules — a favourite JAMB deduction.

points: A flower has sepals, petals, stamens (anther and filament) and carpels (stigma, style, ovary containing ovules).
Insect-pollinated flowers are large, coloured, scented and produce little sticky pollen; wind-pollinated flowers are small, dull and produce much light pollen.
Pollination transfers pollen to the stigma; fertilisation is the later fusion of gametes inside the ovule.
The pollen tube grows down the style, and double fertilisation forms both the embryo and the endosperm.
The ovary becomes the fruit and each ovule becomes a seed; dispersal by wind, animals, water or explosive action reduces competition with the parent.
